steps.title: Spectators
steps.body: People who watch sporting events, either at the venue in person or through media coverage. Spectators are a vital part of the sporting experience, providing atmosphere, revenue and motivation for performers.

steps.title: Hooliganism
steps.body: Disorderly, aggressive and violent behaviour by spectators at sporting events, most commonly associated with football. Hooliganism involves organised groups of fans who engage in fighting, vandalism and intimidation, often planning confrontations in advance.

steps.title: PE Exam Tips — Spectator Behaviour and Hooliganism
steps.body: 1. For Spectator Behaviour and Hooliganism questions, use subject-specific terminology precisely 2. Support every point with specific evidence or examples 3. Show balanced analysis — consider different perspectives before reaching a conclusion 4. Link your understanding of Spectator Behaviour and Hooliganism to real-world contexts where possible 5. For longer answers, plan your response to address all parts of the question

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain three positive effects of spectators on sport. | Describe three causes of hooliganism and explain how each contributes to spectator disorder. | Explain how banning orders work and evaluate their effectiveness in reducing hooliganism.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always balance positive and negative effects of spectators - examiners want both Know three causes of hooliganism and at least three prevention strategies Explain HOW each strategy works, not just what it is Banning orders = legal orders, not just "being banned" - use the correct term Alcohol restrictions: specific rule = no alcohol in view of the pitch in English football The Taylor Report and all-seater stadiums are key historical context for football
